en.name: AeroSwift
en.subtitle: Flight and airport board
en.short_description: Track a flight, read an airport board, and save the ones you fly.
en.description:
AeroSwift is a flight tracker with one job: tell you where an aircraft is and when it is going to land, without an account and without noise.

WHAT IT DOES
• Search a flight by callsign and open a detail view with altitude, aircraft, route, and scheduled versus actual times.
• Open any airport's board and read its arrivals and departures over a window you choose.
• Save the flights you follow so they are one tap away next time.
• A route diagram and a status chip summarise the leg at a glance.

ABOUT THE DATA
AeroSwift ships with an offline sample data set so the app is fully navigable the moment you install it. Switch to live data from the OpenSky Network in Settings — the endpoints AeroSwift uses need no key and no sign-up. A banner in the app always tells you which source you are looking at, so you are never guessing whether a number is real.

NO ACCOUNT
There is no login, no profile, and nothing to subscribe to. Saved flights and your data-source choice stay on the device.

review_information.notes:
Thanks for reviewing AeroSwift.

AeroSwift is a flight tracker. There is no account, no sign-in and no purchase, and the app requests no system permissions at all — no location, no camera, no notifications. All four tabs are reachable the moment it launches.

IMPORTANT — the default build opens on sample flights on purpose. lib/core/env.dart sets the data source to "sample", so the first thing you see is a red banner reading "SAMPLE DATA — these are not real flights" plus a SAMPLE badge on every row. That is deliberate labelling, not a dead feed. Live data is one tap away in Settings and needs no key and no sign-up.

Test instructions:
1. Launch the app. It opens on Search with the sample-data banner across the top. Tap one of the example chips (UA1691, SFO–LHR, BA286, Lufthansa, JFK–LAX), or type a flight number, a route or an airline name.
2. Open a result for the detail view: altitude, aircraft type, registration, a route diagram, a status chip, and scheduled versus actual times. Fields the source cannot supply are shown as unavailable rather than invented.
3. Save a flight, then open the Watchlist tab. Saved flights are kept in shared_preferences on the device.
4. Open the Airports tab, pick an airport and read its arrivals and departures. The look-back window (2, 4, 8, 12 or 24 hours) is set in Settings.
5. Open Settings and choose "OpenSky Network" under Data source. The banner changes to say the data is live and names the source. This is the only step that touches the network.
6. With the live source selected, repeat steps 1–4. OpenSky's anonymous endpoints are rate-limited and serve roughly the last 24 hours only, so a query can legitimately come back empty or as an error card. The app reports that instead of quietly substituting sample data — please do not read it as a crash.

Privacy:
• Data collected: Nothing about you. There is no account and no profile. Saved flights, the chosen data source, the home airport and the board window are written to shared_preferences on the device.
• Network: None in the default sample configuration — the app is fully usable in airplane mode. If you switch the source in Settings, the app calls opensky-network.org directly, anonymously, with no credentials.
• Location: Not requested and not used. There is no location plugin in the build; an airport table from OurAirports (public domain) is bundled at assets/data/airports.psv so codes resolve and routes can be drawn with no network.
• Tracking: None. Crash reporting is Firebase Crashlytics only; there is no advertising or analytics SDK, and the app does not read the advertising identifier, so no App Tracking Transparency prompt appears.

If you need anything else, please email contact@safecodeg.com and we will respond within one business day.
